timeline.body:
Motivation:

[DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH)](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8484) wraps DNS queries inside HTTP request and sends it over HTTPS to make sure queries are secure in transit.

Modification:

Added DoHQueryEncoder, DoHResponseEncoder and DoHDecoder
Added DoHClient Example

Result:
Encoding DnsQuery to HTTP Request using DoHQueryEncoder.

Encode DnsResponse to HTTP Response using DoHResponseEncoder.

Decoding DnsQuery from HTTP Request and DnsResponse from HTTP Response using DoHDecoder.

Fixes #9091.
Can one of the admins verify this patch?

timeline.body: TIOLI: Useful to include url at this point so an unexpected value can be traced back.

HTTP/2 is the minimum recommended protocol here, HTTP/1.1 is not a great fallback

Should this be optional/configurable?

https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8484#section-5.2

reply.body:
I did think about this but `RECOMMENDED` does not enforce (as per my best knowledge). If it was `MUST` then HTTP/1.1 was not allowed.

Please correct if I'm wrong.
@slandelle You have any idea about this `RECOMMENDED` thing? I am also confused now.

My reading, is that if you fallback to HTTP/1.1 then likely you have a very active bottleneck in your system and using DNS over HTTPS will effectively be broken for real world cases. Yes it works, but if something like a intermediate proxy is dropping you down from HTTP/2 to HTTP/1.1 then clients may either want to be aware, notified, or make it configurable.

I guess you can restrict in SslContextBuilder.forClient

I completely agree with that. HTTP/1.1 will ruin the performance. DoT can shine out in that case but out of context for now. RFC says `RECOMMENDED` along with `MINIMUM` HTTP/2.

I ran queries over HTTP/1.1 and they were successful (both Cloudflare and Google DNS).

timeline.body: What's the plan for querying A and AAAA records here? Is it enough that a client can take this library and make a A query and a AAAA query a take the first result?

reply.body:
Client can pass whatever Record type he wants. All we do is take the DNS data from DnsQuery and full it into HTTP request (in URL in case of GET request and in the body in case of POST).

Lemme add few more queries as well for better insights.

Basically I'm curious how this fits into a Netty based server pipeline that needs to do DNS lookups?  This example makes it clear what it looks like to write a simple command line that does IPv4 lookups.

timeline.body: What happens here with dns.google? Is the plan use system DNS for this?

reply.body: `dns.google` does not support GET request for native DoH query. Only JSON API based GET query is supported. But for a POST request, `dns.google` works perfectly fine.
Sorry, I meant that in order to use DoH for queries, you first rely on using system DNS.  Is there a plan here?  Or clients should configure around this in non example code.

Nice point. Yes, if a client uses `dns.google`, it'll be resolved via system DNS that could be using native UDP/TCP.

One possible workaround would be using direct IP Address like:
```java
Channel channel = b.connect("8.8.8.8", 443).sync().channel();
```

However, let's put the worst-case scenario. A client wants to connect to "dns.google" and sends a request to ISP DNS for `dns.google` IP address. Even if ISP sends a malicious IP address (let's say 300.300.300.300, for example purpose), connection over TLS would not be successful because ISP defined IP address doesn't have a valid X.509 certificate for `dns.google`. Unless Client machine has malicious CA installed too, we can trust any DNS query over native UDP/TCP.

This was part of why I've used vague terms like "real world", if the aim is to avoid possibly tainted DNS infrastructure, then a client (say running on an Android device) may have compromised CA certs on device (not in the app).  One of the reasons that certificate pinning exists for the actual service (non dns) HTTP requests.  

This is not a blocking topic, more raising ambiguities around why and how people would use this.  I don't have an answer here.  It's probably best left out of scope for the encoder PR and assume clients don't just enable "dns.google over DoH" and assume everything is now secure.

I can include the certificate pinning or strict certificate check but it will go out of context since it's more of TLS / HTTPS thing.
Clients are free to configure `SslContext`. For certificate pinning, we can have an optional configuration for this.
More than happy for this to be out of scope, just wanted to raise it for discussion.
Maybe we need more examples to demonstrate DoH better.

timeline.body:
It seems like you are ignoring the cache headers which the RFC documents cases when they are relevant to processing.  e.g. Age header.

Are these concerns out of scope of the initial PR?

https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8484#section-5.1

reply.body: Cache Headers are useful if we have some HTTP Caching layer. We're not using any caching here at all and people are free to use custom caching solution for native DnsQuery. So caching is not a concern for now.

The decoder is currently incomplete and broken if caching is implemented by any server. You may want to add "no-cache" to the encoder to make it clear you have skipped any caching for now.

```
DoH clients MUST account for the Age response header field's value
   [RFC7234] when calculating the DNS TTL of a response.  For example,
   if an RRset is received with a DNS TTL of 600, but the Age header
   field indicates that the response has been cached for 250 seconds,
   the remaining lifetime of the RRset is 350 seconds.  This requirement
   applies to both DoH client HTTP caches and DoH client DNS caches.

   DoH clients can request an uncached copy of a HTTP response by using
   the "no-cache" request Cache-Control directive (see Section 5.2.1.4
   of [RFC7234]) and similar controls.  Note that some caches might not
   honor these directives, either due to configuration or interaction
   with traditional DNS caches that do not have such a mechanism.
```

I suspect this might be a first pass requiring a second when you go to use this for real. Or follow up with fixes, and you get "real world" enhancement requests.

It's unclear to make from the example code how this would work in a realistic codebase, and it avoids some of the tricky topics like http response headers by not looking at them.  Obviously things like happy eyeballs are completely out of scope, but a more interesting follow up example would be how to use this to implement something like a small reverse proxy.
